stations.title: Measure blood pressure
stations.subtitle: Palpate first. Listen second. Report clearly.
objectives: Prepare the subject and cuff correctly
Sequence palpatory and auscultatory measurement
Recognise Korotkoff endpoints and the auscultatory gap
Calculate and report pulse pressure and approximate MAP
essentials: Cuff pressure is an indirect estimate of arterial pressure, reported in mmHg.
At rest, support the bare arm at heart level; support the back and keep feet flat and legs uncrossed. Avoid conversation during measurement.
Palpation estimates systolic pressure; it does not reliably provide diastolic pressure.
For routine adult auscultation, first Korotkoff sound is systolic pressure; disappearance is diastolic pressure. If sounds persist, follow the specific protocol and document this.
An auscultatory gap is a temporary loss of sounds followed by their return. It can cause a falsely low systolic or falsely high diastolic reading if misidentified.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent, allow rest and position the subject
steps.why: Position and muscle activity alter the measurement; comfort reduces avoidable variability.

steps.action: Select the cuff from the arm circumference/device markings; locate the brachial artery
steps.why: An unsuitable cuff changes pressure transmission and can bias the result.

steps.action: Estimate systolic pressure using the radial pulse, then fully deflate
steps.why: This guides the later inflation target and helps prevent missing a high systolic pressure across a silent gap.

steps.action: Position the stethoscope over the brachial artery; reinflate to the protocol margin above the estimate
steps.why: A common teaching margin is 20–30 mmHg above the estimate—not a fixed 170 or 300 mmHg for everyone.

steps.action: Deflate slowly, about 2–3 mmHg per second, and identify first sound and disappearance
steps.why: Fast deflation can skip the true endpoints. Watch the gauge while listening.

steps.action: Release the cuff, record SBP/DBP, arm and position; repeat according to protocol
steps.why: A complete report is more useful than an isolated number; repeated measurements require an appropriate pause.

traps.wrong: Inflate every cuff to 300 mmHg.
traps.right: Use the palpatory estimate and a suitable margin. The handwritten note is not a universal procedure.

traps.wrong: The first quiet interval is always diastolic pressure.
traps.right: Sounds may return after an auscultatory gap; follow the full sequence.

worked.title: 120/80 mmHg at rest
worked.formula: PP = SBP − DBP; MAP ≈ DBP + PP/3
worked.working: PP = 40 mmHg; MAP ≈ 80 + 40/3 = 93 mmHg. The MAP shortcut is approximate and most appropriate at a normal resting heart rate.

recall.prompt: Why do palpation before auscultation?
recall.answer: To estimate systolic pressure and avoid mistaking the return of sounds after a gap for the true systolic endpoint.

recall.prompt: What should the written result include?
recall.answer: Systolic/diastolic pressure in mmHg, arm and position; note relevant measurement conditions and repeat readings.

stations.title: Find and explain heart sounds
stations.subtitle: Four listening areas. Two essential sounds.
objectives: Locate the four standard valve auscultation areas
Explain the origin and timing of S1 and S2
Use the stethoscope and describe findings systematically
Distinguish listening areas from anatomical valve positions
essentials: Aortic: right second intercostal space at the sternal edge. Pulmonary: left second intercostal space at the sternal edge.
Tricuspid: left lower sternal border, commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space. Mitral: apex, left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line in a typical adult.
S1 is associated with mitral/tricuspid closure at the beginning of ventricular systole. S2 is associated with aortic/pulmonary closure at the beginning of ventricular diastole.
These are listening areas, not a diagram of exactly where the valves lie. Sound transmission determines where particular sounds are best heard.
Know what S3 and S4 relate to—rapid filling and atrial contraction—but do not assume your file confirms a full murmur-diagnosis station.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent and ensure appropriate exposure/privacy
steps.why: Accurate landmarking must be combined with respectful examination.

steps.action: Find the sternal angle and count the intercostal spaces
steps.why: Do not estimate V1/V2 or valve areas merely from the nipples or collarbone.

steps.action: Listen systematically at aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid and mitral areas
steps.why: A repeatable sequence reduces omissions.

steps.action: Identify S1 and S2 before describing extra sounds
steps.why: The relationship to systole and diastole is more informative than a vague description of a noise.

steps.action: Select the stethoscope side and apply appropriate pressure
steps.why: The diaphragm is used for higher-frequency sounds; a lightly applied bell helps with low-frequency sounds.

steps.action: State your observations and limitations
steps.why: Do not invent a murmur diagnosis if the station only asks for normal heart sounds.

traps.wrong: Left second intercostal space = tricuspid.
traps.right: It is the pulmonary area. The handwritten BP note mislabels it.

traps.wrong: S1 means aortic valve opening.
traps.right: S1 is associated with AV-valve closure; ordinary valve opening is not S1.

worked.title: An examiner points to the left second intercostal space
worked.working: Answer: pulmonary auscultation area. Do not call it tricuspid, and do not imply the valve itself sits directly beneath the stethoscope.

recall.prompt: What closes for S1? For S2?
recall.answer: S1: mitral and tricuspid. S2: aortic and pulmonary.

recall.prompt: What are the four sites without looking?
recall.answer: Right 2nd ICS; left 2nd ICS; left lower sternal border; apex at left 5th ICS/midclavicular line.

stations.title: Record and interpret an ECG
stations.subtitle: Placement → calibration → rate → rhythm → axis.
stations.source: ECG Appl Physio Class 7.ppt + ECG Eng Appl Physio Assignment.ppt
stations.sourceRange: Main slides 5–30, 36, 52–61; all four assignment slides
objectives: Position ten electrodes to obtain twelve leads
Read paper speed, gain, waves and intervals
Calculate rate and assess sinus rhythm
Determine frontal axis and recognise standard lead territories
essentials: A lead is an electrical view; an electrode is a physical contact. Four limb electrodes plus six chest electrodes produce the standard 12-lead ECG.
V1: right 4th ICS; V2: left 4th ICS; V4: left 5th ICS/midclavicular line; V3 halfway between V2 and V4. V5 anterior axillary and V6 midaxillary, both level with V4.
At 25 mm/s, one small horizontal box is 0.04 s and one large box is 0.20 s. Standard gain is 10 mm/mV; always inspect the actual calibration.
P: atrial depolarisation; QRS: ventricular depolarisation; T: ventricular repolarisation. PR is measured from P onset to QRS onset; the course normal range is 0.12–0.20 s.
For normal sinus rhythm, assess rate, regularity, P-wave morphology, P-to-QRS relationship and PR consistency. One positive P wave in lead II alone is not a complete rhythm assessment.

Axis: I+/aVF+ lies in 0° to +90°. I+/aVF− requires lead II to separate a normal mildly leftward axis from left axis deviation. An equiphasic lead suggests a perpendicular axis; use another lead to choose the direction.
Standard territories: inferior II/III/aVF; septal V1/V2; anterior V3/V4; lateral I/aVL/V5/V6. A single ST/T change does not establish a clinical diagnosis in isolation.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent, ensure privacy and prepare relaxed skin contact
steps.why: Movement and poor contact create artefact; correct identification belongs on the recording.

steps.action: Apply labelled limb electrodes and accurately landmark V1–V6
steps.why: Cable colours vary between conventions; use electrode labels and your local system.

steps.action: Check paper speed and gain before recording
steps.why: Timing and amplitude calculations depend on calibration.

steps.action: Inspect quality, then identify P, QRS and T
steps.why: Do not interpret artefact as a rhythm disturbance.

steps.action: Calculate rate and assess the five rhythm features
steps.why: For an irregular rhythm use a timed strip or a mean R–R interval, not a single short interval.

steps.action: Determine axis and report findings in a consistent sequence
steps.why: Use I/aVF with lead II refinement, or the equiphasic method. State uncertainty rather than guessing.

traps.wrong: Divide 60 by the number of small boxes.
traps.right: Convert boxes into seconds first: at 25 mm/s, mean RR = boxes × 0.04 s.

traps.wrong: V3/V4 are septal because slide 60 says so.
traps.right: This is a slide-label error: V3/V4 are conventionally anterior.

traps.wrong: Place limb electrodes on bony prominences because the older video shows this.
traps.right: The video description corrects this: avoid bony prominences and use the proper limb sites.

worked.title: Regular trace
worked.working: Four large boxes between R waves: 300/4 = 75 beats/min.

worked.title: Course irregular-rate example
worked.working: Mean of 22, 14 and 18 small boxes = 18. RR = 18 × 0.04 = 0.72 s. Rate ≈ 83 beats/min. A longer suitable recording improves the estimate.

worked.title: Equiphasic aVR
worked.working: Candidates are −60° and +120°. Predominantly positive I with negative aVF supports the −60° direction; use the actual trace rather than assuming one candidate.

recall.prompt: Why is V4 placed before V3?
recall.answer: V3 is positioned halfway between the already established V2 and V4 locations.

recall.prompt: I is positive and aVF negative: is this always pathological LAD?
recall.answer: No. Check lead II; a positive II can indicate an axis between −30° and 0°, within the usual normal range.

recall.prompt: What is the local assignment asking?
recall.answer: Rhythm with the five-rule approach, a recording-setting adjustment, irregular rate and equiphasic axis. Attempt all four slides without looking at the machine’s printed answer.

stations.title: Read a spirometry trace
stations.subtitle: Technique matters. Scales matter just as much.
objectives: Explain an acceptable forced-expiration manoeuvre
Identify measurable lung volumes on a calibrated trace
Calculate corrected VC and percentage of predicted
Calculate FEV1/FVC and interpret patterns cautiously
essentials: Explain and demonstrate the manoeuvre: maximal inspiration, tight mouth seal and a rapid, forceful expiration continued to the required endpoint. A cough, leak, hesitant start or early stop may invalidate measurements.
TV is the quiet-breathing excursion; IRV is additional inspiration above a normal inspiration; ERV is additional expiration below normal expiration. VC = IRV + TV + ERV.
Simple spirometry does not measure residual volume, and therefore does not directly determine FRC or TLC.

The course trace uses 1 cm/s horizontally and 100 cc between adjacent horizontal lines in the demonstrated setup. Screen resizing is not a physical ruler calibration—use the printed grid/labelled scale.
The worked course example uses corrected VC = measured VC × 1.1. That factor is supplied for its conditions, not universal.
FEV1 is expired volume in the first second; FVC is total forced expired volume. VC and FVC are related but not interchangeable labels in every setting. Use the denominator requested by the exercise.
A reduced ratio supports airflow obstruction. A low FVC with a preserved ratio suggests possible restriction, but restriction requires confirmation of reduced TLC. Poor effort can also reduce FVC.
The slides use 80–120% predicted VC and a >75% ratio as simplified classroom conventions. These are not universal clinical cut-offs for every age and reference population.

steps.action: Check suitability with the supervisor and explain the test
steps.why: Clinical contraindications, infection control and comfort matter; do not stop medication without instructions.

steps.action: Use the correct reference information and device calibration
steps.why: Predicted values depend on the chosen reference equation/table; use the one supplied in the exam.

steps.action: Coach a maximal inspiration and forceful complete expiration with a good seal
steps.why: A weak start lowers early flow/volume; a leak loses measured air.

steps.action: Check acceptability and repeatability according to the lab protocol
steps.why: Three attempts are not automatically three acceptable results.

steps.action: Read the trace using its time and volume scales
steps.why: Do not assume a rising pen means inspiration: the device may record expired volume in that direction.

steps.action: Calculate, show units and interpret the pattern with its limitations
steps.why: An apparent restrictive pattern is not proof of low TLC.

traps.wrong: Apply 1.1 to every spirometry result.
traps.right: Use the stated correction for that exercise; some recordings are already corrected.

traps.wrong: Low FVC proves restriction.
traps.right: It suggests possible restriction; reduced TLC is needed to confirm it, and poor manoeuvre quality must be excluded.

traps.wrong: Use literal centimetres measured on a resized screen.
traps.right: Use the trace’s supplied grid calibration or the original printed scale.

worked.title: Course VC example
worked.formula: % predicted = corrected measured VC / predicted VC × 100
worked.working: 2500 mL × 1.1 = 2750 mL. 2750/3410 × 100 = 80.6%, approximately 81%, within the course’s stated band.

worked.title: Volume and ratio drill
worked.working: IRV 2.0 L + TV 0.5 L + ERV 1.0 L = VC 3.5 L. If forced FEV1 is 2.4 L and FVC 3.0 L, their ratio is 80%. Do not mix litres and millilitres.

recall.prompt: What cannot basic spirometry measure?
recall.answer: Residual volume, and therefore capacities containing it: FRC and TLC.

recall.prompt: Which seven values are requested in slide 24?
recall.answer: TV, IRV, ERV, VC, VC/predicted VC%, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC%, followed by a judgement about lung tissue/airway resistance.

recall.prompt: Why might an early stop be misleading?
recall.answer: It can underestimate FVC and distort the ratio; assess quality before interpreting physiology.

stations.title: Count red blood cells
stations.subtitle: Know the volume before memorising the multiplier.
objectives: Choose RBC-preserving diluent and dilution
Identify the RBC counting area and boundary convention
Derive RBC concentration from counted volume
Recognise loading and sampling errors
equipment: Improved Neubauer chamber and correct coverslip
Approved RBC diluent and pipetting device
Prepared blood sample under laboratory supervision
essentials: Dilution makes a dense cell suspension countable; the diluent must preserve RBCs. The course names Hayem’s fluid for RBCs.
At 1:200 dilution, count five groups in the central 1-mm² square: four corner groups and the centre group. Each group contains 16 small squares.
Each group is 0.2 × 0.2 mm = 0.04 mm². Five groups give 0.20 mm²; with 0.1-mm depth, volume = 0.020 mm³ = 0.020 µL.
Concentration = N × dilution / volume. For this setup only: N × 200 / 0.020 = N × 10,000 cells/µL.
Use a consistent boundary rule: include two adjacent edges and exclude the opposite two. Otherwise cells shared by squares may be counted twice.
Locate the grid at low power, then use the course’s 40× objective for RBC counting. Total magnification includes both ocular and objective.

steps.action: Identify the chamber, coverslip, sample and approved diluent
steps.why: The correct coverslip establishes the intended chamber depth; improvised substitution alters volume.

steps.action: Prepare the prescribed dilution using a pipetting device and mix
steps.why: Concentration calculations require the actual dilution, and uneven mixing biases sampling.

steps.action: Load by capillary action without bubbles, overflow or underfilling
steps.why: An evenly filled known volume is necessary for a valid count.

steps.action: Locate the central grid and select the five groups
steps.why: Do not confuse these groups with the four large WBC corner squares.

steps.action: Count systematically using the same boundary convention
steps.why: Consistent traversal and edge rules prevent omission and double counting.

steps.action: Calculate cells/µL, report the dilution and inspect plausibility
steps.why: A very unexpected value should prompt checks of dilution, grid selection and loading before biological interpretation.

traps.wrong: Each central medium group is 0.25 mm wide.
traps.right: It is 0.2 mm: five groups span 1 mm. Slide 9 contains a dimension typo.

traps.wrong: Multiply every RBC count by 10,000 regardless of dilution.
traps.right: Derive the multiplier from dilution and counted volume; different setups need different factors.

recall.prompt: Why is the volume 0.020 µL?
recall.answer: Five groups × 0.04 mm² × 0.1 mm depth = 0.020 mm³; 1 mm³ equals 1 µL.

recall.prompt: Why not use Türk’s fluid?
recall.answer: Its acetic acid lyses RBCs, which is useful for WBC counting but destroys the cells you want to count here.

images.caption: Four corner groups and the middle group of the central grid are selected—not the four large WBC squares.

stations.title: Count white blood cells
stations.subtitle: Four corner squares. A different dilution.
objectives: Explain Türk’s fluid and WBC dilution
Identify WBC counting volume
Calculate and report total WBC concentration
Distinguish total count, differential and preventable errors
essentials: Türk’s fluid uses acetic acid to lyse RBCs and a stain to make leukocyte nuclei easier to see. Do not confuse its purpose with RBC preservation.
The course’s standard example uses 1:20 dilution and counts four large corner squares. Each is 1 mm²; at 0.1-mm depth, combined volume = 0.4 µL.
For that example: WBC/µL = N × 20/0.4 = N × 50. If dilution is 1:10, the factor is 25 for the same area/depth.
The total WBC count is a concentration. The differential identifies the proportions of different WBC types; one cannot replace the other.
Check mixing, chamber loading, boundary convention and selected area before interpreting an unexpectedly high or low result.

steps.action: Confirm the WBC dilution and reagent
steps.why: Do not use the RBC procedure’s 1:200 dilution by habit.

steps.action: Mix and load the correctly assembled chamber
steps.why: The coverslip and proper loading establish the known depth and even distribution.

steps.action: Locate all four large corner squares
steps.why: These differ from the central RBC groups.

steps.action: Count with consistent borders and a systematic path
steps.why: Avoid counting cells twice where squares share a boundary.

steps.action: Multiply by dilution and divide by counted volume
steps.why: The volume, rather than memorisation alone, explains the factor.

steps.action: Report cells/µL or ×10^9/L and review quality
steps.why: 6000/µL equals 6.0 × 10^9/L; it does not mean 6000%.

traps.wrong: N × 50 is valid for all dilutions.
traps.right: It is valid for 1:20 dilution and four 1-mm² squares at 0.1-mm depth.

traps.wrong: A differential percentage tells the total WBC concentration.
traps.right: A percentage needs a total WBC count to obtain an absolute subtype count.

worked.title: The course’s count of 120
worked.working: 6000 WBC/µL = 6.0 × 10^9/L. Show the area, depth and dilution so the multiplier is auditable.

recall.prompt: Why do RBCs disappear in this preparation?
recall.answer: The acetic acid in Türk’s fluid lyses them so leukocytes are easier to count.

recall.prompt: How does 1:10 dilution change the multiplier?
recall.answer: With the same 0.4-µL counted volume: 10/0.4 = 25, rather than 50.

stations.title: Identify the five WBC types
stations.subtitle: Read nucleus, cytoplasm and granules—not just colour.
objectives: Recognise granulocytes by morphology
Distinguish lymphocytes and monocytes
Calculate a differential and an absolute subtype count
Explain systematic smear sampling and source limitations
essentials: Neutrophil: segmented/multilobed nucleus and relatively fine pale granules. Eosinophil: often bilobed nucleus with conspicuous orange-red granules. Basophil: coarse dark granules that may obscure the nucleus.

Lymphocyte: typically a dense round nucleus with a relatively narrow rim of cytoplasm in a small mature cell. Monocyte: larger cell, folded/kidney-shaped nucleus and more abundant grey-blue cytoplasm.
Real cells vary. Use nuclear shape, chromatin, size and granules together; a single colour cue or every large cell being called a monocyte is unreliable.
The course exercise counts 100 WBCs, so the tally for each type equals its percentage. With a different total, calculate type/total × 100.
Course reference percentages: neutrophils 45–70, lymphocytes 20–40, monocytes 3–8, eosinophils 2–4, basophils 0–2. These are the deck’s ranges, not universal reference intervals.
Absolute subtype count = total WBC × fraction. A high percentage does not necessarily imply a high absolute count.
The deck demonstrates identification more fully than smear preparation/staining. Do not infer an exact stain timing or reagent recipe that is not supplied.

steps.action: Check slide identity and locate a suitable monolayer
steps.why: Overlapping thick areas and extreme feather-edge distortion make identification less reliable.

steps.action: Focus with the appropriate objective using the laboratory protocol
steps.why: Use immersion oil only with an oil-compatible objective; protect the slide and microscope.

steps.action: Traverse systematically rather than selecting attractive cells
steps.why: A consistent pattern limits duplicate counting and selection bias.

steps.action: Classify each WBC from combined morphological features
steps.why: Distinguish cells using nucleus and cytoplasm, not guesswork from colour alone.

steps.action: Tally the specified number and calculate percentages
steps.why: The denominator is the actual number of WBCs counted.

steps.action: Report the differential with uncertainty and absolute counts if available
steps.why: A percentage result must not be presented as cells/µL.

traps.wrong: Basophils must show an easily visible nucleus.
traps.right: Their coarse dark granules can obscure it.

traps.wrong: 60% neutrophils always means neutrophilia.
traps.right: Assess the absolute count and the appropriate reference interval.

worked.title: Local 100-cell exercise
worked.working: Slide 17: N 59, L 28, M 8, E 4, B 1. Total 100, therefore 59%, 28%, 8%, 4%, 1%. Cover the bottom answer and recount before checking.

recall.prompt: Eosinophil versus basophil?
recall.answer: Eosinophil: prominent orange-red granules, often bilobed nucleus. Basophil: coarse dark-purple granules, sometimes obscuring the nucleus.

recall.prompt: Monocyte versus small mature lymphocyte?
recall.answer: Monocyte: larger, more cytoplasm and folded nucleus. Small lymphocyte: dense round nucleus with a narrow cytoplasmic rim.

stations.title: Read hematocrit / PCV
stations.subtitle: Separate the layers. Align the reader. Exclude the seal.
objectives: Explain packed-cell volume and specimen choice
Recognise layers and centrifuge safety
Read a hematocrit reader and calculate PCV
Identify causes of biased readings and interpret cautiously
equipment: Suitable capillary tube and approved sample
essentials: Hematocrit is the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells, commonly expressed as a percentage. It is not an RBC number concentration.
The source uses anticoagulated blood or an appropriate heparinised capillary for fresh capillary blood. Avoid a clotted or haemolysed specimen.
After centrifugation: packed RBCs below, a thin buffy coat of WBCs/platelets, and plasma above. The anticoagulated upper layer is plasma, not serum.
Align 0 at the base of the packed RBC column and 100 at the top of the plasma column. Read the top of packed RBCs without including the buffy coat.
For a ruler calculation: RBC-column length / total blood-column length × 100. Neither the seal nor empty air belongs in these lengths.
The deck lists adult male 42–54% and female 38–46%; these are course ranges and vary with laboratory/population. Dehydration can increase hematocrit without increasing total RBC mass.

steps.action: Confirm suitable anticoagulated sample and correct tube
steps.why: A clot prevents a representative packed-cell-volume measurement.

steps.action: Prepare and seal the capillary under supervision
steps.why: A secure seal prevents leakage; exact filling and handling follow the lab SOP.

steps.action: Balance the centrifuge and orient sealed ends outward as instructed
steps.why: Balanced loading and secure closure are essential; speed/time depend on the machine’s validated protocol.

steps.action: Wait for a complete stop before accessing tubes
steps.why: Do not open or handle a moving rotor.

steps.action: Identify the three layers and align the reader
steps.why: Base of RBCs = 0; top plasma = 100; top RBCs = result.

steps.action: Report PCV with sample/technical limitations
steps.why: Do not interpret a single value without hydration, method and reference context.

traps.wrong: Include buffy coat in packed RBC height.
traps.right: Buffy coat contains WBCs and platelets, not the red-cell numerator.

traps.wrong: The top layer must be serum.
traps.right: In this anticoagulated specimen it is plasma.

worked.title: Ruler calculation
worked.formula: PCV = RBC length / total blood length × 100
worked.working: RBC column 18 mm; total blood column 40 mm: PCV = 45%. Exclude seal and air from the measurement.

recall.prompt: What makes up the buffy coat?
recall.answer: White blood cells and platelets.

recall.prompt: Why can dehydration raise PCV?
recall.answer: A reduced plasma volume raises the red-cell fraction even without an increase in total RBC mass.

images.caption: Recognise the seal, packed RBCs, buffy coat and plasma. The slide’s machine settings are not universal.

stations.title: Distinguish bleeding and clotting time
stations.subtitle: Different endpoints. Different parts of haemostasis.
objectives: Distinguish primary haemostasis from fibrin clot formation
Recognise the bleeding-time endpoint and course convention
Recognise capillary and slide clotting-time endpoints
Handle method dependence and ambiguous instructions safely
equipment: For recognition: timer, filter paper, approved lancet
Capillary or slide apparatus as specified
Protective equipment and sharps disposal under supervision
essentials: Bleeding time assesses cessation of bleeding after a standardised injury and reflects platelet–vessel interactions in primary haemostasis. It is not a direct platelet count.
Clotting time follows formation of a clot/fibrin under the method’s conditions. It is different from bleeding cessation and is not identical to PT or aPTT.
The course’s Duke-style BT description uses serial filter-paper observations and a 1–3 minute usual range. Do not copy the slide’s puncture depth as a safe instruction.

Capillary CT endpoint: first visible fibrin thread between separated capillary ends. The deck quotes 3–7 min. Slide CT uses a specified clot endpoint and quotes 4–10 min. Reference ranges belong to the named method.
The course slides conflict about the capillary CT timer start and contain an unclear checking interval. These are unresolved SOP questions, not details to guess for practical performance.
Temperature, technique, contact surface and endpoint selection can change results. Learn these as historical/classroom practicals; do not treat them as a comprehensive modern bleeding-risk screen.

steps.action: Observe the specified endpoint without disrupting it

steps.action: Record elapsed time, units and method
steps.why: A number without method is difficult to compare with a reference interval.

steps.action: Discuss limitations rather than diagnosing from one result
steps.why: Neither a normal BT nor CT excludes every bleeding disorder.

traps.wrong: BT and CT measure the same endpoint.
traps.right: BT: bleeding cessation. CT: clot/fibrin formation under a specified method.

traps.wrong: Follow the source’s ambiguous timer wording without clarification.
traps.right: Confirm the SOP start point and observation interval; they affect the result.

traps.wrong: Practise finger-pricks or breaking blood-filled glass at home.
traps.right: Practise recognition and explanation at home; invasive work and sharps require supervision.

worked.title: Report the method, not only the number
worked.formula: Result = elapsed time + unit + named method
worked.working: For a hypothetical course capillary CT of 5 min: report the capillary method and timing convention. It lies within that deck’s 3–7 min range; this does not rule out every haemostatic disorder.

recall.prompt: What is the capillary clotting-time endpoint?
recall.answer: First visible fibrin thread at the separated capillary ends, with timing defined by the laboratory’s SOP.

recall.prompt: Why can a heparinised tube be useful for PCV but unsuitable for CT?
recall.answer: PCV needs the sample not to clot. CT is observing clot formation, so an anticoagulant would interfere.

recall.prompt: What must be clarified before this station?
recall.answer: The actual BT/CT method, approved equipment, timer start, checking interval and reference range.
